strengths: The paper presents a clean and genuinely novel theoretical insight: perturbing only one player's payoff preserves the linearity of the other player's objective, allowing exact equilibrium recovery, in contrast to symmetric perturbation.

Theorem 3.1 provides a rigorous, previously missing impossibility result showing that symmetric perturbation almost never recovers the exact equilibrium, clarifying an important gap in the literature on regularized/perturbed learning dynamics.

Theorem 3.3 and its accompanying Corollary 4.2/Theorem 4.1 give a complete theoretical package: exact equilibrium invariance under small asymmetric perturbation plus an O(1/t) last-iterate convergence rate for a concrete gradient algorithm (AsymP-GDA), with full, careful proofs in the appendix.

Extensive empirical validation across normal-form games (BRPS, M-Ne, biased matching pennies, biased RPS) and six extensive-form games via CFR+ variants, consistently showing that the asymmetric variant reaches near machine-precision NashConv while the symmetric variant plateaus at a nonzero gap.

The paper anticipates and addresses a natural limitation (small permissible μ when α is small) by proposing an adaptive-anchoring extension (Ada-AsymP-GDA) with its own convergence guarantee and empirical validation.
Reproducibility is well supported: pseudocode, hyperparameters, compute details, and (claimed) code release are all provided; the appendix is thorough and self-contained.
weaknesses: The practical usability of the method hinges on the constant α in Theorem 3.3/Corollary 4.2, which is only known to exist and "depend on X*" without an explicit characterization or estimation procedure; users cannot easily determine how small μ must be in a new game without prior knowledge of the equilibrium set.

For extensive-form games (Section 5), no theoretical convergence guarantee is given for AsymP-CFR+; the claims there rest solely on empirical evidence on relatively small OpenSpiel benchmarks (Kuhn/Leduc poker, small Goofspiel/Liar's Dice instances), leaving open whether the benefits persist in larger, more realistic games.

The core theoretical results are specific to bilinear/normal-form (or sequence-form) two-player zero-sum games; it is unclear how the approach and analysis would extend to more general convex-concave saddle-point problems or multi-player settings, limiting the generality of the contribution relative to its motivating claims about "min-max problems" broadly.

Theorem 3.1's impossibility result is stated only for normal-form games with a unique interior equilibrium not equal to the uniform strategy, which is a fairly narrow class of games; the practical scope of the impossibility claim (e.g., for games with multiple equilibria or boundary equilibria) is not discussed.

The idea of perturbing only one side is a relatively simple structural modification (as the authors themselves note as "a seemingly minor structural change"), and while the theoretical analysis is non-trivial, the conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental relative to the existing symmetric perturbation/regularization literature (e.g., anchoring methods already used by Perolat et al., Abe et al.).

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with the intuition sometimes buried in lengthy derivations (e.g., Theorem 3.1's proof and its discussion); a clearer high-level explanation of why the numerator/denominator terms in the impossibility threshold arise would improve readability.

strengths: The core theoretical insight is elegant and non-trivial: Theorem 3.1 provides a clean impossibility result explaining why symmetric perturbation (widely used in prior work) almost never recovers the exact equilibrium, and Theorem 3.3 gives a clear, intuitive reason (preservation of linearity for the unperturbed player) why asymmetric perturbation avoids this issue.

The last-iterate convergence proof for AsymP-GDA (Theorem 4.1) is technically substantial; the paper correctly identifies and addresses the key difficulty that the asymmetric setting lacks joint strong convexity, and develops a projection-based lower bound (Lemmas F.1-F.7) to compensate.

Empirical results are fairly extensive, covering both normal-form games (with trajectory visualizations, seed-averaged NashConv curves, and comparisons to GDA/OGDA/SymP-GDA) and six extensive-form benchmark games (Kuhn/Leduc Poker, Goofspiel, Liar's Dice) against standard CFR variants.
Good reproducibility practices: full proofs in the appendix, pseudocode for AsymP-CFR+, hardware/hyperparameter details, and submitted code.
The connection drawn between the perturbation framework and practical CFR+-style regret minimization is a nice applied translation of the theoretical idea.
weaknesses: The central practical claim -- that AsymP-GDA converges 'without requiring parameter adjustment' -- is significantly weakened by the fact that the admissible range for µ in Theorem 3.3/Corollary 4.2 depends on the constant α, which is game-dependent, generally unknown, and not computable a priori. In practice a user still cannot verify whether a chosen µ is 'small enough' without already knowing properties of the (unknown) equilibrium set, undermining the tuning-free narrative that motivates the paper.

Remark 4.3 essentially concedes this limitation and proposes an anchoring mechanism (Ada-AsymP-GDA) as a fix, but this reintroduces a new hyperparameter (anchor update interval Tσ) and associated tuning complexity -- the very problem the asymmetric approach was designed to avoid.

For the extensive-form game application (Section 5), no convergence guarantee is provided for AsymP-CFR+; the paper explicitly states this is 'significantly more difficult' and offers only empirical validation. This means the paper's headline theoretical results (Theorems 3.1, 3.3, 4.1) do not actually cover the extensive-form setting where much of the empirical showcase occurs.

Theorem 3.1's impossibility result requires a 'unique interior equilibrium,' a fairly restrictive assumption that excludes many practically important games with boundary or non-unique equilibria (including many extensive-form games solved via CFR variants), limiting the scope of the stated impossibility claim relative to how broadly it is invoked in the introduction.

The paper does not adequately justify the comparative advantage of perturbation-based methods over already-established optimistic algorithms (OGDA, EG, OMWU) that achieve last-iterate convergence without needing to reason about an unknown threshold constant α; the related-work discussion mentions these methods but the experimental comparison to OGDA is relegated to the appendix and is not deeply analyzed.

Experiments are limited to small, synthetic/benchmark games (3x3 matrices, small poker variants); there is no evaluation at larger scale or with function approximation (e.g., neural network strategy representations), despite the introduction motivating the work partly via large-scale games where average-iterate convergence is problematic.

The extensive technical machinery (many lemmas, long proofs) is largely a careful but incremental adaptation of prior last-iterate analysis techniques (e.g., Wei et al. 2021), and the overall level of originality beyond the core asymmetric perturbation idea is moderate.

strengths: A clean and novel negative result (Theorem 3.1): the paper rigorously proves that symmetric payoff perturbation almost never yields the exact equilibrium of the original bilinear game for any fixed perturbation strength, formalizing a limitation that was previously only known qualitatively (O(mu) distance bounds).

The core idea—perturbing only one player's payoff—is simple, well-motivated, and elegantly explained via the near-linearity argument and the accompanying landscape figure (Figure 2), making the mechanism intuitive as well as rigorous.

Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 4.2 provide a full theoretical package: not only equilibrium invariance under small mu, but also a concrete O(1/t) last-iterate convergence rate for a practical gradient algorithm (AsymP-GDA), with a fairly involved and self-contained proof (Appendix F) handling the asymmetric strongly-convex/linear structure.

Strong and broad empirical validation: normal-form game trajectories/NashConv curves, extensive-form game experiments across six standard benchmarks (Kuhn/Leduc Poker, Goofspiel, Liar's Dice) using CFR+ variants, consistently showing that the asymmetric variant reaches near machine-precision NashConv while the symmetric variant plateaus.

Good engineering follow-through: the paper anticipates and addresses the practical concern of small feasible mu via an adaptive anchoring extension (Ada-AsymP-GDA/CFR+) with matching theory and experiments in the appendix.
Reasonable reproducibility: pseudocode, hyperparameters, compute environment, and source code are provided, and the checklist responses are consistent with the paper's content.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.3's practical usability is limited because the threshold on mu depends on the unknown constant alpha and on max over X* of ||x*||, both of which require knowledge of the (unknown) equilibrium/error-bound structure of the game; the paper acknowledges this in Remark 4.3 but the mitigation (anchoring) is validated only empirically without a fully worked-out guidance for choosing mu a priori.

Theorem 3.1's impossibility result is stated specifically for normal-form games with a unique interior equilibrium; extending the formal negative result to general polytope/extensive-form games (sequence-form) is not done, even though the extensive-form experiments implicitly rely on the same intuition — the CFR+ results in Section 5 remain purely empirical with no accompanying convergence proof, which is explicitly acknowledged but nonetheless a gap in the theoretical coverage.

All experiments are on small-to-moderate benchmark games (2-5 actions in normal form; standard small extensive-form testbeds); there is no evaluation on larger, more realistic games (e.g., larger Poker variants or the Stratego-scale settings referenced in the introduction as motivation for perturbation-based methods), leaving open how well the method scales or interacts with function approximation (e.g., neural policy representations) in practice.

The choice of which player to perturb is treated as essentially arbitrary/symmetric-by-convention (perturb x, or perturb y separately to get y*), but the paper does not discuss practical implications of this choice in adversarial or asymmetric-stakes settings, nor whether alternating which player is perturbed could combine benefits or introduce trade-offs.

The convergence rate obtained (O(1/t)) is the same order as prior last-iterate results for constrained bilinear games (e.g., Wei et al. 2021), so while the equilibrium-exactness contribution is novel, the quantitative convergence-rate contribution alone is not a rate improvement over existing baselines; the empirical speed gains, while visually convincing, are not accompanied by a wall-clock or sample-efficiency analysis relative to strong baselines like OGDA/extra-gradient in the normal-form experiments (only GDA/SymP-GDA/OGDA are compared, and OGDA is only shown in the appendix figures).

strengths: The core idea is simple but genuinely novel: perturbing only one player's payoff (rather than symmetrically) yields exact equilibrium invariance for sufficiently small perturbation strength, in contrast to the well-known O(µ) bias of symmetric perturbation. This is a clean conceptual contribution that is likely to be useful to the broader perturbation/regularization-for-games literature.

Theorem 3.1 is well-motivated and its proof cleverly leverages the near-linear growth property of bilinear objectives (from Wei et al. 2021) combined with strong convexity of the added penalty; the intuition is nicely illustrated in Figure 2.

The paper establishes a linear last-iterate convergence rate for AsymP-GDA (Theorem 4.1) despite the asymmetric/non-strongly-convex-concave structure, which is a nontrivial technical result requiring a piecewise-affine/Hoffman's-bound argument (Remark 4.4, Appendix F) rather than standard strong-convexity contraction arguments used in the symmetric case.

A parameter-free variant (Algorithm 1) is provided that retains a linear rate without needing to know the game-dependent constant α, addressing a natural practical concern about the theory (Theorem 4.3), with a full complexity analysis in the appendix.

The new impossibility result for symmetric perturbation (Theorem B.1, Appendix H) is a useful complementary theoretical contribution, giving an exact characterization of when x^µ ≠ x* rather than just an O(µ) bound, strengthening the motivation for the asymmetric approach.

Empirical evaluation is fairly extensive: normal-form games (BRPS, M-Ne, BMP) and five extensive-form games (Kuhn, Leduc, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel variants), with comparisons against a good range of baselines (GDA, OGDA, SymP variants, dilated MWU/GDA/OMWU/OGDA, and CFR-family algorithms), plus sensitivity analyses to µ and trajectory visualizations that build intuition for the invariance regime.
weaknesses: All theoretical results are restricted to the bilinear saddle-point setting; extensions to more general (e.g., convex-concave, Markov game, or neural-network parameterized) settings are only speculated as future work, despite the introduction motivating the approach partly via large-scale/neural-network games and LLM fine-tuning, for which no experiments are provided.

The core theoretical guarantee (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 4.2) depends on an unknown game-dependent constant α; while Algorithm 1 sidesteps needing to know α exactly, its iteration complexity still implicitly depends on α through K, and the practical experiments (e.g., µ=1 in Figure 3/6) do not systematically verify that the chosen µ lies within the theoretical invariance regime for larger/more complex games, leaving a gap between theory and the practical heuristic of picking µ.

Sensitivity results (Figure 7, 8) show that performance degrades once µ exceeds the (a priori unknown) invariance threshold, meaning that outside the parameter-free algorithm, practitioners still face a real tuning burden similar in spirit to (though structurally different from) the symmetric-perturbation case.

All experiments use exact (full-information) gradients; the motivation section explicitly discusses failures of optimistic methods under bandit/noisy feedback (Abe et al. 2022), but no experiments or theory address whether the asymmetric perturbation approach retains its advantages under stochastic gradients, which is an important practical gap.

The impossibility result (Theorem B.1) is stated only for normal-form games with a unique interior equilibrium, which is a restrictive special case; its implications for more general polytope strategy spaces or non-unique/boundary equilibria are not discussed.

The games used in the extensive-form experiments are relatively small (Kuhn, Leduc, small Goofspiel/Liar's Dice variants); no evidence is given about how the method scales to larger games or games requiring function approximation, despite these being the primary motivating use cases in the introduction.

strengths: The central idea—perturbing only one player's payoff in a bilinear saddle-point problem—is a clean, non-obvious observation, and Theorem 3.1 rigorously shows exact equilibrium invariance below a threshold, which is a genuinely surprising structural fact and contrasts nicely with the well-known O(mu) bias of symmetric perturbation.

The paper backs up the motivating claim about symmetric perturbation with a novel formal impossibility result (Theorem B.1/Corollary B.2), which is a useful complementary theoretical contribution beyond just citing prior O(mu) bounds.

The last-iterate linear convergence proof for AsymP-GDA (Theorem 4.1) is technically nontrivial, since it must handle the asymmetric setting where only one player's objective is strongly convex, using a Hoffman's-bound/piecewise-affine argument rather than the standard strong-convexity contraction argument used for symmetric perturbation.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across several normal-form and extensive-form games with tuned baselines (GDA, OGDA, MWU variants, CFR family), including ablations on perturbation strength and trajectory visualizations that make the invariance phenomenon intuitive.

The parameter-free variant (Algorithm 1) elegantly exploits the invariance property to avoid needing to know the game-dependent constant, and is shown to retain a linear rate, improving over the O(1/t) rate of prior decreasing-schedule methods.
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantees are restricted to bilinear games over polytopes with a specific error-bound/sharpness property (borrowed from Wei et al. 2021); the paper does not establish any convergence theorem for the extensive-form (dilated regularizer) variant actually used in Section 5's main experiments, so the flagship empirical results for AsymP-DGDA rest entirely on analogy rather than proof.

The practical significance of the 'linear rate' and 'broad range of mu' claims is undermined by unquantified constants: the threshold alpha in Theorem 3.1 and the contraction constant beta_mu in Theorem 4.1 (derived via Hoffman's bound over a piecewise-affine map) are not characterized in terms of problem dimension or matrix conditioning, and Hoffman constants are well known to potentially be exponentially bad; the paper offers only two small (3x3) game instances as empirical evidence that the invariance regime is 'reasonably wide,' which is thin support for a claim central to the paper's motivation.

The parameter-free algorithm's theoretical guarantee (Theorem 4.3) still depends on alpha through the episode count K and the stopping thresholds, so the practical iteration complexity is not truly independent of the unknown game-dependent constant, despite the algorithm not needing to query it directly; this nuance is underexplained.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the technical machinery (sharpness inequality from Wei et al., Hoffman's bound, piecewise-affine analysis, dilated regularizers from Hoda et al.) is largely assembled from existing tools, and the core algorithmic change relative to symmetric perturbation is a single-line modification (dropping the y-perturbation term); the conceptual contribution is valuable but the technical novelty is more modest than the framing suggests.

Experiments are all on small-scale academic benchmarks (Kuhn/Leduc poker, small Goofspiel/Liar's Dice variants), which is somewhat at odds with the paper's stated motivation involving large-scale games and LLM fine-tuning via preference optimization; no evidence is given that the method scales to such settings or handles stochastic/sampled gradients, which the introduction explicitly flags as a weakness of optimistic methods that this paper's approach is not shown to overcome.

The comparison between AsymP-GDA's linear rate and the O(1/t) rate of Liu et al. [2023] is not entirely apples-to-apples, since the two methods make different structural assumptions/use different stopping criteria, and the paper could more carefully delineate under what conditions this speed advantage materializes in wall-clock or iteration terms in the experiments (e.g., the extensive-form experiments already show competitive but not always dramatically superior performance over DOMWU/DOGDA in some games).

strengths: The core idea—perturbing only one player's payoff rather than both—is simple, elegant, and non-obvious in its consequences. Theorem 3.1 rigorously shows that this asymmetry yields an *exact* equilibrium invariance regime (not merely an O(µ)-approximation as in symmetric perturbation), which is a genuinely novel qualitative improvement over the prior literature (Liu et al. 2023, Abe et al. 2024).

The paper backs up the motivation with a rigorous impossibility result (Theorem B.1) proving that symmetric perturbation essentially never recovers an exact equilibrium for any fixed µ>0 in generic games, which nicely complements and motivates the proposed asymmetric approach.

Theorem 4.1/Corollary 4.2 establish a linear last-iterate convergence rate for AsymP-GDA despite the perturbation being applied to only one player, which is a non-trivial technical result (the proof needs a piecewise-affine/Hoffman's-bound argument since strong convexity alone is insufficient in the asymmetric setting, as explained in Remark 4.4).

A parameter-free variant (Algorithm 1) is provided that removes the need to know the game-dependent constant α while still retaining a linear rate—improving on the O(1/t) rate of comparable decreasing-µ schemes in prior work (Liu et al. 2023).

Broad and careful empirical evaluation: normal-form games (BRPS, M-Ne, BMP) with sensitivity analyses to µ, and extensive-form games (Kuhn, Leduc, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel) compared against a good spread of baselines (OGDA, OMWU, MWU, CFR/CFR+/DCFR/LCFR variants), consistently showing AsymP-(D)GDA converges faster and to an exact equilibrium while SymP variants stall at an approximate one.

The manuscript is well organized, with intuitive geometric illustrations (Fig. 2) clarifying why linearity of the unperturbed player preserves the minimizer, and a full, careful appendix with detailed proofs for all major claims.
weaknesses: The theory is restricted to deterministic bilinear (matrix) games; extension to two-player zero-sum Markov games or general convex-concave problems is only speculated as future work, despite the introduction motivating the work partly via large-scale/RL and bandit-feedback settings where these results are not shown to apply.

The invariance guarantee in Theorem 3.1 depends on an unknown, game-dependent constant α; while the parameter-free algorithm sidesteps needing to know α, it introduces an outer doubling-search loop over µ and requires a target accuracy ε as input, adding practical complexity and an extra layer of tuning/early-stopping thresholds (δ) not fully characterized empirically.

Experiments remain on relatively small/medium games (Kuhn, Leduc, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel with modest sizes); given the paper's motivating discussion of large-scale games and LLM fine-tuning via preference optimization, no experiments probe scalability, stochastic/bandit-gradient settings, or neural-network-parameterized policies, leaving the practical relevance to the motivating large-scale use cases unverified.

The dilated-regularizer extension to sequence-form strategies is used only empirically (Section 5); no convergence guarantee (e.g., linear rate) is proven for AsymP-DGDA analogous to Theorem 4.1, so the theoretical story does not fully extend to the extensive-form experiments presented.

The comparisons rely on hand-tuned hyperparameters per game (Table 4) for all baselines and the proposed method; while stated as tuned for best performance, the tuning protocol/search space is not fully detailed, making it harder to assess fairness robustness of the comparison, especially for optimistic-method baselines that are known to be sensitive to learning rates.
